question: In 2019, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) awarded the 2026 Winter Olympics to Milan and Cortina. The bid file stated that the Olympics would be funded primarily using private capital and, placing sustainability centre stage, make use of existing structures. Over the past few days, construction of the bobsleigh track – a brand new facility – has got under way in Cortina.

Taking up the entire ridge of one of the most beautiful mountains in the Alps, the track is being built in breach of many EU rules. Plans were not submitted for an assessment pursuant to Directive 2011/92/EU, on the grounds that bobsleigh tracks are not listed in the annexes to the directive.

What is more, a forest of larch trees of over 20 000 m2 was felled without a single environmental assessment, despite deforestation being among the activities listed in Annex II to Directive 2011/92/EU.

Lastly, the overall plan for the Olympics works, approved by Prime Ministerial Decree of 8 September 2023, was not submitted for the environmental assessment of plans and programmes provided for in Directive 2001/42/EC, which is needed, inter alia, for the purpose of determining the cumulative effects. In the light of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it not think it ought to step in on this abominable project?
Will it ask Italy for clarification?
answer: Projects of clear-cutting of trees fall under Annex II (1) of the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Directive (2). For such projects, Member States shall determine on a case-by-case examination or using pre-determined thresholds or criteria whether the project shall be made subject to an environmental impact assessment (3).

Under Article 3 of the Strategic Environmental Assessment Directive (4), an environmental assessment shall be carried out for plans and programmes which are likely to have significant environmental effects. This concerns in particular plans and programmes for tourism or land use.

Moreover, based on Article 3 (4) and (5), Member States shall determine whether plans and programmes, other than those referred above, which set the framework for future development consent of projects, are likely to have significant environmental effects, either through case-by-case examination or by specifying types of plans and programmes or by combining both.

In February 2024, the Commission received a complaint on the project in question. This is under assessment and the Commission will decide on the appropriate course of action. Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, Member States are primarily responsible to ensure compliance with EU law, verifying individual cases of potential breach of the relevant rules.

Clear-cutting of trees falls under Point 1(d). Bobsleigh runs are not specifically listed in Annex II, point 12(a) of which only covers ‘ski runs, ski lifts and cable cars and associated developments’. Directive 2011/92/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2011 on the assessment of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment, OJ L 26, 28.1.2012, p.

1-21, as amended by Directive 2014/52/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 April 2014, OJ L 124, 25.4.2014, p. 1-18. Article 4(2). Directive 2001/42/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 June 2001 on the assessment of the effects of certain plans and programmes on the environment, OJ L 197, 21.7.2001, p. 30-37.

In its Article 11, the EIA Directive, as transposed in the Italian law (5), contains specific provisions related to access to justice. In line with its strategic approach on enforcement action (6) the Commission focuses on systemic non-compliance.

Part II of Legislative Decree n. 152 of 3 April 2006, (GU n.88 of 14-04-2006 — Suppl. Ord. n. 96).
